final_proof:
Let \(K\) be a subfield of \(\mathbb C\), and denote its multiplicative identity by \(1_K\). We first verify that \(1_K\) is the usual complex number \(1\). Because a field is not the zero ring, there exists \(a\in K\) with \(a\ne0\). In \(K\), one has \(1_Ka=a\); this equality also holds in \(\mathbb C\), since the operations on \(K\) are the restrictions of those on \(\mathbb C\). Multiplying both sides in \(\mathbb C\) by \(a^{-1}\) yields \(1_K=1\).

Now let \(n\) be any positive integer. Using the inherited addition and \(1_K=1\), we obtain
\[
n\cdot1_K
=\underbrace{1_K+\cdots+1_K}_{n\text{ terms}}
=\underbrace{1+\cdots+1}_{n\text{ terms}}
=n.
\]
The last \(n\) is a strictly positive real number and hence is not the zero element of \(\mathbb C\). Consequently \(n\cdot1_K\ne0\) for every positive integer \(n\). By definition, the characteristic of a field is the least positive integer \(n\) satisfying \(n\cdot1_K=0\), if such an integer exists, and is \(0\) if none exists. Therefore \(\operatorname{char}(K)=0\).
